episodes.173399: A monsoon trough, extending across the Philippines and into the Mariana Islands, brought periods of heavy rain to Guam leading to flooding during the morning of October 11th. Central and southern portions of Guam received on average 4 to 7 inches of rain between 0130ChST and 1400ChST, while northern portions of Guam received 1 to 3  inches of rain between 0300ChST and 1300ChST. The peak of the heavy rainfall was between 0300ChST and 0600ChST, with an automated rain gage in southern Guam (near the village of Umatac) recording 0.72 inches in 15 minutes or an hourly rain rate of 2.88 inches.
episodes.174779: A Tropical Upper Tropospheric Trough combined with an approaching tropical wave. The wave enhanced the moisture content in the atmosphere, and with the instability aloft, conditions became favorable for showers and thunderstorms development across the area.
episodes.174942: Isolated thunderstorms moved east across southeast Arizona during the afternoon. One storm produced a severe wind gust in the Santa Catalina Mountains.
episodes.175072: A broad trough with embedded shortwaves was positioned over the Southwestern US. This led to an active and wet period across West Texas and Southeast New Mexico. During the afternoon of the 10th, thunderstorms developed on the higher terrain of the Davis Mountains and moved east over the Stockton Plateau. One storm became nearly stationary, producing severe weather and flash flooding in and around Fort Stockton. The cost of damage was a rough estimation based on storm reports.

events.narrative: A social media report indicated a landslide at road PR-607 in Barrio Caonillas, Utuado. The road was impassable due to the landslide.

Heavy rainfall across central and southern portions of Guam caused ponding on roadways. Estimates of 4 to 6 inches fell across the Pago watershed. The Pago River gage showed Pago river starting at a height around 2 feet at 0250ChST quickly climbing to over 5 feet at 0315ChST, and peaking at 14.28 feet at 0505ChST before slowly decreasing and not dropping below 5 feet until 0740ChST. Route 4 near Pago Bay (located just north of the Pago River crossing) had reports of water over the road, and though it never officially closed, traffic stopped for a time as people felt passage was unsafe.

Heavy rainfall across central and southern portions of Guam caused ponding on roadways. Via group chats and social media, the office received reports of water covering the northbound lanes of Route 1 (called locally as Marine Corps Drive) near Polaris Point, located south of the village of Piti. The Mount Chachao rain gage near Piti reported a total of 4.69 inches with 2.89 inches falling between 0245ChST and 0530ChST.

Heavy rainfall across central and southern portions of Guam caused ponding on roadways. Rain gages across southern Guam showed about 4 to 7 inches fell during the morning hours. A bridge located where Joutan Lane meets up with Route 4 had water over the road and debris was piled up along the side of the bridge and road. Removal of debris is estimated to cost about $500.
A report from the 911 call center indicated flooding due to heavy rain at road PR-167 in direction from Bayamon to Naranjito.
A report received from the 911 call center indicated flooding at Calle 39, Reparto Teresita in Bayamon due to heavy rainfall in the area.
A report from the 911 call center indicated a flooded house at Calle 14 in Guaynabo, due to heavy rain.
A report from the 911 call center indicated multiple cars trapped due to flooding in Ave. Lomas Verdes in Guaynabo. Rescue operations were ongoing.
A post from social media indicated flooding of multiple roads and houses along Urb. Santa Rosa in Bayamon. This information was confirmed by emergency managers.
Scout Camp RAWS measured a thunderstorm wind gust of 60 mph.

Heavy rainfall across central and southern portions of Guam caused ponding on roadways. Estimates of 4 to 6 inches fell across the Pago watershed. The Pago River gage showed Pago river starting at a height around 2 feet at 0250ChST quickly climbing to over 5 feet at 0315ChST, and peaking at 14.28 feet at 0505ChST before slowly decreasing and not dropping below 5 feet until 0740ChST. Route 4 near Pago Bay (located just north of the Pago River crossing) had reports of water over the road, and though it never officially closed, traffic stopped for a time as people felt passage was unsafe. Moderate rainfall then kept Pago river between 4 and 5 feet from 0740ChST to 1135ChST as the Route 4 near Pago Bay still had ponding on the road, but traffic was moving and improving at this time.
Pecos County Airport measured a 61 mph thunderstorm wind gust.
Hail is along Highway 285 north of Fort Stockton.
At 6:18 it was still hailing in Fort Stockton.
There were several water rescues in Fort Stockton. Schools and hospitals were flooded in town.
